inboxMessages.subject: Did marketing cause the sales lift?
inboxMessages.body: Revenue is up 14% in the same period that paid-search spend increased. I need one sentence for the board: can we say the campaign caused the lift?

choices.text: Say the campaign caused the lift because the timing matches.
choices.feedback: Timing and correlation are not enough for a causal claim.
choices.followUp: Rhea replies: “Finance is challenging that statement. What evidence do we actually have?”

choices.text: Report the association, quantify the lift, and say causality needs an experiment or stronger design.
choices.feedback: Strong analyst response: useful evidence without overstating what the data proves.
choices.followUp: Rhea replies: “Good. Put the observed association on the slide and add the experiment plan underneath.”

choices.text: Refuse to discuss marketing until a perfect randomized experiment exists.
choices.feedback: You protected against overclaiming, but you also threw away useful observational evidence.
choices.followUp: Rhea replies: “I still need the best answer we can support today.”

inboxMessages.subject: Your dashboard and my ledger disagree
inboxMessages.body: Your dashboard shows ₹14.8M revenue. Finance has ₹13.4M for the same month. The review starts in 30 minutes. Which number should we present?

choices.text: Use the larger number because it is better for the meeting.
choices.feedback: Choosing the favorable number without reconciliation destroys trust.
choices.followUp: Kabir replies: “We cannot defend that. Find the definition difference.”

choices.text: Average the two values and label it an estimate.
choices.feedback: Averaging inconsistent definitions creates a third number that is not a source of truth.
choices.followUp: Kabir replies: “That does not reconcile either source.”

choices.text: Reconcile date window, status filters, tax/returns treatment and refresh time before presenting either number.
choices.feedback: Correct. Conflicting reports are a definition and lineage problem before they are a presentation problem.
choices.followUp: Kabir replies: “Good. I’ll hold the slide until we agree the metric definition.”

inboxMessages.subject: Conversion fell after the redesign
inboxMessages.body: Signup-to-activation conversion dropped from 41% to 36% after the new onboarding flow launched. Can I roll it back now?

choices.text: Roll it back immediately because conversion is lower.
choices.feedback: The signal matters, but you have not checked sample size, instrumentation, mix or uncertainty.
choices.followUp: Maya replies: “Could traffic mix have changed too?”

choices.text: Check instrumentation, segment mix, sample size and uncertainty, then recommend rollback only if the decline remains decision-relevant.
choices.feedback: Strong: validate measurement first, then combine effect size and uncertainty with business cost.
choices.followUp: Maya replies: “Great. Break it down by device and acquisition channel before the decision.”

choices.text: Ignore the drop because five percentage points is too small to matter.
choices.feedback: A 5-point change can be commercially large. Practical significance depends on scale and context.
choices.followUp: Maya replies: “That change represents thousands of users.”

inboxMessages.subject: Email me the high-risk customer list
inboxMessages.body: Send me the full customer-level risk file with names, phone numbers and flags. I’ll forward it to the regional heads.

choices.text: Send the full file because the VP requested it.
choices.feedback: Authority does not remove privacy, minimum-necessary and access-control obligations.
choices.followUp: Arvind replies: “Compliance is asking why sensitive fields were distributed broadly.”

choices.text: Provide the minimum necessary fields through an approved access-controlled channel and confirm the purpose/recipients.
choices.feedback: Correct: minimize sensitive data and use governed distribution.
choices.followUp: Arvind replies: “Use the secure workspace and omit contact details. Good catch.”

choices.text: Refuse all risk analysis because customer data is sensitive.
choices.feedback: Privacy controls should enable legitimate analysis, not block it completely.
choices.followUp: Arvind replies: “We still need the portfolio review—just handle it correctly.”

inboxMessages.subject: Delete the weird rows
inboxMessages.body: There are a few huge values in the file. Please delete all outliers so the average looks normal.

choices.text: Delete every value beyond 1.5×IQR automatically.
choices.feedback: IQR is useful for detection, not automatic proof that a value is wrong.
choices.followUp: Nikhil replies: “One of the deleted rows was our largest enterprise customer.”

choices.text: Flag statistical outliers, verify business context/source evidence, then choose robust summaries or exclusions with documentation.
choices.feedback: Correct: unusual is not the same as erroneous.
choices.followUp: Nikhil replies: “Keep the enterprise account and show median plus P90 beside the mean.”

choices.text: Keep every row and never investigate outliers.
choices.feedback: You avoided arbitrary deletion but missed a necessary quality check.
choices.followUp: Nikhil replies: “Some of those rows really are import errors.”

inboxMessages.subject: Can we say staffing caused the wait-time drop?
inboxMessages.body: Median wait fell after staffing changed, but several other operational changes happened that week. Leadership wants a causal statement.

choices.text: State that staffing caused the improvement.
choices.feedback: The timing is suggestive but multiple simultaneous changes create confounding.
choices.followUp: Dr. Isha replies: “Clinical operations says routing changed too. Reframe this.”

choices.text: Report the observed improvement, list competing changes, and recommend a stronger comparison/design before attributing cause.
choices.feedback: Correct: useful operational evidence with causal restraint.
choices.followUp: Dr. Isha replies: “Good. Segment by day and department, then propose a controlled comparison.”

choices.text: Say no conclusion of any kind can be made.
choices.feedback: You can still describe the observed change even when causal attribution is uncertain.
choices.followUp: Dr. Isha replies: “I need the descriptive result and the caveat together.”

inboxMessages.subject: Give me the exact peak-week volume
inboxMessages.body: Capacity planning needs one exact shipment number for festival week. Finance does not want a range.

choices.text: Give the point forecast with no uncertainty because leadership asked for one number.
choices.feedback: Operational plans built on false precision are fragile.
choices.followUp: Arjun replies: “What happens if we are 10% high or low?”

choices.text: Provide the point forecast plus downside/base/upside scenarios, assumptions and capacity actions for each.
choices.feedback: Strong planning response: a forecast becomes useful when uncertainty is connected to actions.
choices.followUp: Arjun replies: “Use the base for budget, but staff the contingency trigger at the upside threshold.”

choices.text: Refuse to forecast because the future is uncertain.
choices.feedback: Uncertainty is exactly why structured forecasts and scenarios are needed.
choices.followUp: Arjun replies: “We still have to make a capacity decision.”

inboxMessages.subject: Why do our active-user numbers disagree?
inboxMessages.body: Product says 82k MAU. Finance says 69k. Both teams swear their SQL is correct.

choices.text: Pick the query with fewer lines because it is easier to audit.
choices.feedback: Query length does not resolve a metric-definition conflict.
choices.followUp: Leena replies: “The teams are still arguing about what counts as active.”

choices.text: Define activity event, time window, account/user grain, test-account exclusions and timezone, then reconcile both queries to that definition.
choices.feedback: Correct: metric governance starts with a shared definition and grain.
choices.followUp: Leena replies: “We found Finance excludes internal accounts and Product does not. Standardize it.”

choices.text: Average 82k and 69k for the dashboard.
choices.feedback: Averaging incompatible definitions creates a meaningless number.
choices.followUp: Leena replies: “That number has no business definition.”

inboxMessages.subject: The executive report takes 14 seconds to load
inboxMessages.body: The page has 38 visuals, a wide flat table and several complex measures. Leadership wants it faster without losing the decision story.

choices.text: Add more pages but keep all 38 visuals on the landing page.
choices.feedback: The landing page remains cognitively and computationally heavy.
choices.followUp: Sara replies: “It is still slow and executives still cannot find the headline.”

choices.text: Reduce landing-page visuals, remove unused columns, restore a star schema, simplify expensive measures and profile remaining bottlenecks.
choices.feedback: Correct: improve model and visual design before micro-optimizing.
choices.followUp: Sara replies: “Load time is down and the executive hierarchy is clearer.”

choices.text: Convert every numeric field to text to reduce calculations.
choices.feedback: That damages modeling, compression and calculation behavior.
choices.followUp: Sara replies: “The model is now larger and several measures broke.”

inboxMessages.subject: Need a number in 10 minutes
inboxMessages.body: What is customer churn this quarter? Just send me a number—no time for definitions.

choices.text: Send the first churn number you can query.
choices.feedback: A fast wrong metric is still wrong. Churn depends on denominator, cohort and period definition.
choices.followUp: Rhea replies: “Customer Success has a different number. Which one is right?”

choices.text: Confirm the existing approved churn definition, state the number plus denominator/window, and flag if the definition is not settled.
choices.feedback: Strong: move quickly without abandoning metric governance.
choices.followUp: Rhea replies: “Perfect. Put the definition in the footnote and send it.”

choices.text: Tell the CEO analytics cannot work under deadlines.
choices.feedback: Good analysts manage urgency while protecting the minimum quality bar.
choices.followUp: Rhea replies: “I need a defensible answer, not a lecture.”

inboxMessages.subject: My revenue doubled after the JOIN
inboxMessages.body: I joined orders to customer_tags and revenue is exactly 2.1× higher. The SQL runs without errors. Can I publish it?

choices.text: Publish it because syntactically valid SQL is trustworthy.
choices.feedback: A query can run perfectly and still be logically wrong.
choices.followUp: Dev replies: “I found customers with multiple tags. Each order is repeated.”

choices.text: Check join cardinality, duplicate keys and before/after row counts; aggregate tags or choose the intended grain before summing revenue.
choices.feedback: Correct senior-review behavior: validate grain and cardinality before trusting totals.
choices.followUp: Dev replies: “Fixed. Revenue now reconciles to the source ledger.”

choices.text: Divide the doubled revenue by 2.1.
choices.feedback: A correction factor hides the modeling error and will fail when tag counts change.
choices.followUp: Dev replies: “The factor changed on another day.”

inboxMessages.subject: Three requests, one analyst
inboxMessages.body: You have capacity for one deep analysis today: (A) a cosmetic dashboard redesign, (B) a suspected revenue-recognition mismatch before earnings review, or (C) a new low-impact chart requested for next month.

choices.text: Prioritize the revenue-recognition mismatch because decision risk and immediacy are highest.
choices.feedback: Correct prioritization: impact, risk and deadline outrank cosmetic preference.
choices.followUp: Board Office replies: “Finance found a filter defect before the pack went out.”

choices.text: Prioritize the cosmetic dashboard redesign because executives see it most.
choices.feedback: Visibility does not automatically equal business risk or urgency.
choices.followUp: Board Office replies: “The financial mismatch reached the meeting unresolved.”

choices.text: Start all three and finish none deeply.
choices.feedback: Spreading limited capacity across every request can increase overall decision risk.
choices.followUp: Board Office replies: “We needed one issue resolved, not three half-finished.”

handbookEntries.title: SELECT + WHERE
handbookEntries.shortcut: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition
handbookEntries.formula: SELECT order_id, revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed';
handbookEntries.example: Return only completed order IDs and revenue.
handbookEntries.whenUse: When you need a specific subset of rows/columns.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not use SELECT * by default in production analysis when only a few fields are needed.

handbookEntries.title: GROUP BY
handbookEntries.shortcut: Change output grain, then aggregate.
handbookEntries.formula: SELECT segment, SUM(revenue) FROM orders GROUP BY segment;
handbookEntries.example: One result row per customer segment.
handbookEntries.whenUse: When the business question asks for totals/averages/counts by a dimension.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not GROUP BY just to remove duplicates; fix the grain/key problem instead.

handbookEntries.title: JOIN cardinality
handbookEntries.shortcut: Define expected 1:1, 1:M or M:M before joining.
handbookEntries.formula: orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
handbookEntries.example: Many orders to one customer dimension.
handbookEntries.whenUse: When attributes/measures live in related tables.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not join on descriptive text or ignore duplicate keys.

handbookEntries.title: Window functions
handbookEntries.shortcut: Calculate across related rows without collapsing detail.
handbookEntries.formula: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY revenue DESC)
handbookEntries.example: Rank customers inside each segment.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Ranks, running totals, LAG/LEAD, moving averages.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not replace a simple GROUP BY with a window if row-level detail is unnecessary.

handbookEntries.title: XLOOKUP
handbookEntries.shortcut: Key → matching value from another table.
handbookEntries.example: Map customer_id to segment.
handbookEntries.whenUse: When you have a stable lookup key.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not use an unstable descriptive label as the key.

handbookEntries.title: SUMIFS
handbookEntries.shortcut: Sum a measure only for rows meeting conditions.
handbookEntries.example: Completed North-region revenue.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Fast conditional summaries in structured spreadsheets.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: For large repeatable pipelines, SQL/Pandas may be more auditable.

handbookEntries.title: Pivot table
handbookEntries.shortcut: Rows/Columns = dimensions; Values = measures.
handbookEntries.formula: Rows: Region | Columns: Status | Values: SUM Revenue
handbookEntries.example: Revenue matrix by region and status.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Fast exploratory summaries and business reviews.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not trust a pivot until source grain and aggregation are understood.

handbookEntries.title: Absolute references
handbookEntries.shortcut: $ locks a row/column when copying formulas.
handbookEntries.example: Apply one tax/discount rate stored in F1 to many rows.
handbookEntries.whenUse: When one parameter should stay fixed while a formula is copied.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not lock references that should move row-by-row.

handbookEntries.title: Row grain
handbookEntries.shortcut: Before cleaning, answer: what does one row represent?
handbookEntries.formula: Order line grain → unique key may be order_id + line_id
handbookEntries.example: Repeated order_id can be valid when an order has many lines.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Before deduplication, joins and aggregation.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Never delete duplicates before defining the business key.

handbookEntries.title: Missing values
handbookEntries.shortcut: NULL ≠ zero ≠ unknown ≠ not applicable.
handbookEntries.formula: Impute only when business semantics justify it.
handbookEntries.example: No support tickets may mean 0; missing plan name means Unknown.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Any dataset with blanks/nulls.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not fill every numeric null with zero automatically.

handbookEntries.title: Dates & types
handbookEntries.shortcut: Validate meaning first, then normalize types.
handbookEntries.example: 01/02/2026 is ambiguous without locale context.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Before time filtering, joins and time-series analysis.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not silently guess day/month conventions.

handbookEntries.title: Join/reconciliation QA
handbookEntries.shortcut: Compare before/after row counts, keys and totals.
handbookEntries.formula: source rows → joined rows → unmatched keys → duplicate keys → total reconciliation
handbookEntries.example: A many-to-many join can double revenue without any SQL error.
handbookEntries.whenUse: After merges/joins and before publishing metrics.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not assume a successful join is logically correct.

handbookEntries.title: Mean vs median
handbookEntries.shortcut: Use median for a typical value when extreme values distort the mean.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Skewed distributions or strong outliers.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Median can hide total magnitude when totals/means are the actual business quantity.

handbookEntries.title: Standard deviation
handbookEntries.shortcut: Spread in the original unit.
handbookEntries.example: 40±4 minutes is more consistent than 40±20 minutes.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Quantify variability around a mean when appropriate.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: For heavily skewed data, pair with median/percentiles.

handbookEntries.title: Confidence interval
handbookEntries.shortcut: Effect estimate + plausible uncertainty range.
handbookEntries.example: Conversion lift +2.1 pp, 95% CI [0.4, 3.8].
handbookEntries.whenUse: Communicate precision of estimates.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not interpret a 95% CI as 95% probability the fixed true value is inside after observing data.

handbookEntries.title: p-value
handbookEntries.shortcut: Compatibility with a null model—not probability the null is true.
handbookEntries.formula: Compare p to pre-specified alpha, but also report effect size.
handbookEntries.example: p=0.18 → insufficient evidence to reject at 0.05; not proof of no effect.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Formal hypothesis-testing workflows with valid assumptions.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not use p<0.05 as the only definition of business importance.

handbookEntries.title: Power & MDE
handbookEntries.shortcut: Design the experiment around the smallest effect worth detecting.
handbookEntries.formula: Power depends on baseline, MDE, alpha, variance and sample size.
handbookEntries.example: If +1 pp is commercially meaningful, size the test to detect about that effect.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Before running A/B tests.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not choose sample size after looking at results just to reach significance.

handbookEntries.title: Filter rows
handbookEntries.shortcut: Boolean mask → keep only qualifying rows.
handbookEntries.example: Completed orders only.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Subsetting analysis data.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not overwrite raw data before validating the filter logic.

handbookEntries.title: groupby + agg
handbookEntries.shortcut: Split by dimension, summarize measures.
handbookEntries.example: Total MRR per segment.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Grouped KPIs and summaries.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not aggregate before deciding the intended output grain.

handbookEntries.title: merge validation
handbookEntries.shortcut: Merge on keys; validate cardinality and unmatched rows.
handbookEntries.example: Attach account segment to transactions.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Combining related DataFrames.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not merge on non-unique keys without understanding row multiplication.

handbookEntries.title: Missing-value workflow
handbookEntries.shortcut: Inspect → understand meaning → fill/drop/flag deliberately.
handbookEntries.example: Measure missing plan rate before choosing treatment.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Any incomplete DataFrame.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not call fillna(0) globally.

handbookEntries.title: Star schema
handbookEntries.shortcut: Facts measure events; dimensions describe them.
handbookEntries.example: Revenue stays in FactOrders; region in DimCustomer.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Most analytical semantic models.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Avoid one giant flat table when it creates duplication/ambiguity.

handbookEntries.title: Measure vs calculated column
handbookEntries.shortcut: Measure = dynamic filter-context KPI; column = row-level stored value.
handbookEntries.example: MRR should change with month/segment slicers.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Measures for aggregates, ratios and report KPIs.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not store a grand total repeatedly in a calculated column.

handbookEntries.title: CALCULATE
handbookEntries.shortcut: Evaluate a measure under modified filter context.
handbookEntries.example: Count only on-time shipments while retaining route/month filters.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Conditional measures and context transformation.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not use CALCULATE without understanding the filter context it changes.

handbookEntries.title: Date table
handbookEntries.shortcut: Continuous calendar → reliable time intelligence.
handbookEntries.example: Prior-month and YoY measures work even when fact dates are sparse.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Any time-series semantic model.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not rely only on month-name text in the fact table.

handbookEntries.title: Row-level security
handbookEntries.shortcut: Restrict which rows each user can see.
handbookEntries.example: Regional managers see only their region; executives see all.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Governed reports with role-based data access.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not treat hidden visuals as security.

handbookEntries.title: Gross margin %
handbookEntries.shortcut: Gross profit normalized by revenue.
handbookEntries.example: Revenue can grow while margin falls if discount/cost rises faster.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Compare profitability across products/periods of different scale.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not infer cash generation from gross margin alone.

handbookEntries.title: Funnel conversion
handbookEntries.shortcut: Each stage rate needs a clear denominator.
handbookEntries.formula: Stage conversion = next-stage users / current-stage users
handbookEntries.example: 200 trials → 80 activations = 40%.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Diagnose drop-off across ordered user stages.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not compare rates with inconsistent stage definitions.

handbookEntries.title: Net Revenue Retention
handbookEntries.shortcut: Existing-base revenue after churn, contraction and expansion.
handbookEntries.example: 105% NRR can coexist with customer churn if expansion offsets losses.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Recurring-revenue health.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not use NRR alone to understand logo churn or acquisition.

handbookEntries.title: CAC, LTV & payback
handbookEntries.shortcut: Acquisition cost must be evaluated against customer value and recovery time.
handbookEntries.example: ₹5k CAC with ₹1k monthly gross profit ≈ 5-month simple payback.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Growth economics and channel decisions.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not use revenue-only LTV when gross margin/cost materially changes economics.

handbookEntries.title: Line vs bar
handbookEntries.shortcut: Line for ordered time; bar for category comparison.
handbookEntries.example: 12-month revenue trend = line; region revenue = bars.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Simple comparisons with a clear decision.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not use pie/donut for long time series.

handbookEntries.title: Scatter plot
handbookEntries.shortcut: Two numeric variables → relationship pattern.
handbookEntries.formula: x = possible driver; y = outcome; each point = entity/period
handbookEntries.example: Marketing spend vs conversions by campaign.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Relationships, clusters, non-linearity and outliers.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not infer causality from the plotted association alone.

handbookEntries.title: Cohort heatmap
handbookEntries.shortcut: Start group × age/period.
handbookEntries.formula: Rows = acquisition cohort | Columns = months since signup | Cell = retention %
handbookEntries.example: Compare retention decay across signup months.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Retention and lifecycle analysis.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not mix calendar month with customer age without labeling clearly.

handbookEntries.title: Decision story
handbookEntries.shortcut: Finding → evidence → driver → action → monitor.
handbookEntries.formula: What changed? Why might it matter? What should we do next?
handbookEntries.example: Late SLA +4 pp, concentrated on two routes → investigate capacity/handoffs; monitor P90.
handbookEntries.whenUse: Executive and operational dashboards.
handbookEntries.whenNotUse: Do not add commentary that claims causes the data cannot support.

metricCases.title: Revenue Growth That Is Getting Worse

choices.text: The company is clearly healthier because revenue is up 20%.
choices.feedback: Top-line growth can hide deteriorating unit economics and retention.

choices.text: Growth is accelerating but its quality is deteriorating; investigate discount/mix, acquisition efficiency and churn before scaling further.
choices.feedback: Correct. Read the metrics as a system, not as isolated wins/losses.

choices.text: Stop all marketing immediately.
choices.feedback: The warning signs matter, but the data supports diagnosis and targeted action before a blanket stop.

choices.text: No risk; NRR above 100% means retention is excellent.
choices.feedback: Expansion can mask meaningful logo churn and concentration.

choices.text: Expansion offsets losses, but customer churn and concentration make the result fragile; segment expansion and track dependency on the top account.
choices.feedback: Correct. NRR needs logo and concentration context.

choices.text: NRR is useless and should be removed.
choices.feedback: NRR is useful; it just should not be interpreted alone.

choices.text: Conversion improved, so the business must be growing.
choices.feedback: Conversion improved, but traffic and AOV moved against revenue.

choices.text: Funnel efficiency improved, but lower traffic and basket value offset it; quantify each driver before changing the channel plan.
choices.feedback: Correct driver-based interpretation.

choices.text: AOV is the only metric that matters.
choices.feedback: Revenue is driven by multiple interacting components.

choices.text: Wait time problem is solved because the median improved.
choices.feedback: The long tail remains unchanged and capacity pressure persists.

choices.text: Typical experience improved, but severe waits did not; segment high-wait periods and address Saturday capacity.
choices.feedback: Correct: median and P90 answer different operational questions.

choices.text: Ignore the median because only P90 matters.
choices.feedback: Both central tendency and tail experience are useful.

metricCases.title: Shipping Cost Is Up—Efficiency Is Better

choices.text: Shipping efficiency worsened because average cost rose.
choices.feedback: Absolute cost rose alongside a larger workload.

choices.text: Absolute cost rose, but normalized cost efficiency improved; review weight/route mix before cutting spend.
choices.feedback: Correct: normalize the cost driver before judging efficiency.

choices.text: Cost/kg falling proves total profit increased.
choices.feedback: Profit needs revenue and other costs; normalized shipping cost alone cannot prove it.

metricCases.title: NPA Ratio Down, NPA Amount Up

choices.text: Credit quality definitely improved because the ratio fell.
choices.feedback: The denominator grew faster, while absolute NPAs and new delinquencies still rose.

choices.text: The ratio improved partly because the loan book expanded; investigate absolute NPAs and new delinquency cohorts before declaring lower risk.
choices.feedback: Correct denominator-aware interpretation.

choices.text: Ratios should never be used in risk analysis.
choices.feedback: Ratios are useful when read alongside amounts and denominator changes.

choices.text: Celebrate MAU growth and stop analysis.
choices.feedback: Reach increased while depth and core adoption weakened.

choices.text: Separate acquisition-driven reach from engagement quality; cohort new users and inspect activation/core-feature adoption.
choices.feedback: Correct: breadth and depth can move in opposite directions.

choices.text: Sessions/user alone proves the product is failing.
choices.feedback: One engagement metric is not enough to make that conclusion.

choices.text: PAT is up, so cash flow does not matter.
choices.feedback: Accounting profit and cash conversion can diverge materially.

choices.text: Why is working capital absorbing cash despite higher profit? Investigate receivables, inventory and payment timing.
choices.feedback: Correct: connect profit to cash conversion and working capital.

choices.text: Inventory growth proves demand will rise.
choices.feedback: Inventory growth may reflect demand planning, overstock or timing; it is not proof of future sales.

reviewCases.title: Junior Analyst: Revenue Doubled After JOIN
reviewCases.artifact: SELECT SUM(o.revenue) FROM orders o JOIN customer_tags t ON o.customer_id=t.customer_id;

choices.text: Join cardinality and duplicate customer_tags keys.
choices.feedback: Correct. Many tags per customer can duplicate each order before aggregation.

choices.text: SQL capitalization.
choices.feedback: Formatting is not the cause of doubled revenue.

choices.text: Divide the result by 2.
choices.feedback: A correction factor hides the underlying grain error.

choices.text: The mean is distorted by an extreme value; compare median/percentiles.
choices.feedback: Correct. Typical-value language needs a robust summary here.

choices.text: The mean formula is mathematically invalid.
choices.feedback: The arithmetic can be correct while the business interpretation is poor.

choices.text: Remove the ₹12,500 order automatically.
choices.feedback: First verify whether it is a valid high-value order.

reviewCases.title: Junior Analyst: Satisfaction Bar Chart
reviewCases.artifact: Product A = 98, Product B = 96. Bar axis starts at 95.

choices.text: The truncated bar baseline visually exaggerates a two-point difference.
choices.feedback: Correct. Bar length is interpreted relative to its baseline.

choices.text: Use more colors.
choices.feedback: Color does not fix the distortion.

choices.text: Bars cannot show percentages.
choices.feedback: Bars can show percentages; the baseline is the issue.

reviewCases.title: Junior Analyst: p = 0.08 Means No Effect
reviewCases.artifact: “p=0.08, therefore the scheduling change definitely has no effect.”

choices.text: Call the result inconclusive at the chosen threshold and report effect size/uncertainty.
choices.feedback: Correct. Failure to reject is not proof of no effect.

choices.text: Change alpha to 0.10 after seeing the result so it becomes significant.
choices.feedback: Post-hoc threshold changes inflate false-positive risk.

choices.text: Delete the test from the report.
choices.feedback: The test can still be informative when interpreted correctly.

reviewCases.title: Junior Analyst: Bidirectional Everything
reviewCases.artifact: The model has five bidirectional many-to-many relationships. Slicers change unrelated totals.

choices.text: Return to explicit fact/dimension grain and simpler one-to-many filter paths.
choices.feedback: Correct. Simplify the model before adding more filter paths.

choices.text: Add more bidirectional relationships.
choices.feedback: That usually increases ambiguity.

choices.text: Hide the slicers.
choices.feedback: That hides the symptom rather than fixing the model.

reviewCases.title: Junior Analyst: Workbook Total Looks Right
reviewCases.artifact: SUM uses B2:B450, but new data now runs to B612. Several rows are hidden by an old filter.

choices.text: The workbook is not refresh-safe; fix the range/table design and clear/validate filters.
choices.feedback: Correct. Static ranges and stale filters create silent reporting errors.

choices.text: The total looks close enough.
choices.feedback: A management workbook needs traceable completeness.

choices.text: Increase decimal precision.
choices.feedback: Precision is unrelated to missing rows.

reviewCases.title: Junior Analyst: Customer Risk CSV in Email
reviewCases.artifact: Attachment contains name, phone, address and risk flag sent to 40 recipients.

choices.text: Use minimum necessary fields and an approved access-controlled distribution method.
choices.feedback: Correct. Privacy and access control are part of analytical professionalism.

choices.text: Compress the CSV first.
choices.feedback: Compression does not solve data-minimization or access risk.

choices.text: Rename the file confidential.csv.
choices.feedback: A filename is not a security control.

reviewCases.title: Junior Analyst: Exact Forecast Promise
reviewCases.artifact: “Peak-week volume will be exactly 112,430 shipments.” No interval, assumptions or scenarios.

choices.text: Add assumptions, forecast error/uncertainty and decision scenarios.
choices.feedback: Correct. Forecasts support decisions; they are not certainties.

choices.text: Add more decimal places.
choices.feedback: More precision can make false certainty worse.

choices.text: Remove all forecasts because forecasts can be wrong.
choices.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to plan with scenarios, not avoid forecasting.

stories.title: The Dashboard That Grew Revenue and Lost Money
stories.setup: A fast-growing marketplace celebrated 28% revenue growth. The team optimized only for gross merchandise value.
stories.turningPoint: Finance added discount depth, gross margin, return rate and fulfilment cost to the review. The highest-growth category was destroying contribution margin.
stories.lesson: Top-line growth is not the same as healthy growth. Metric trees and unit economics prevent local optimization.
takeaways: Use a driver tree, not one headline KPI.
Check whether the incentive encourages the wrong behavior.

stories.title: NRR Looked Great Until One Customer Left
stories.setup: A SaaS company reported NRR above 105% for four quarters.
stories.turningPoint: One enterprise customer generated most expansion. Logo churn was rising quietly. When that account contracted, NRR fell sharply.
stories.lesson: A strong aggregate can hide concentration and weak breadth. Pair NRR with logo retention and expansion concentration.
takeaways: Ask what can reverse the headline metric.

stories.title: The Convenient Risk Proxy
stories.setup: A team found that one customer attribute was highly correlated with manual-review flags.
stories.turningPoint: Governance review showed the attribute was a weak proxy with fairness and data-quality concerns.
stories.lesson: Predictive association does not automatically justify a high-stakes policy. Governance is part of analytics.

stories.title: The Average Wait Improved—Patients Still Complained
stories.setup: Average and median wait time fell after an operations change.
stories.turningPoint: P90 wait remained extremely high during weekend peaks. The typical experience improved while the worst experiences did not.
stories.lesson: Central tendency can hide operational tails. Percentiles often matter for service reliability.

stories.title: The Route That Looked Expensive
stories.setup: One route had 18% higher average shipping cost and was targeted for cuts.
stories.turningPoint: The route handled much heavier shipments and cost per kilogram was actually lower than the network average.
stories.lesson: Normalize by workload before judging efficiency.
takeaways: Separate absolute cost from unit efficiency.
